title: Generative AI Use and Two-Wave Change in Well-Being and Ill-Being: A Pre- and Post-generative AI Era Panel Study
authors: Hyunhee Kang, Young Min Baek
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly spreads, concerns about its impact on users’ mental health have surged. However, previous studies have yielded contradicting results owing to theoretical and methodological limitations. To address these gaps, this study investigates how generative AI adoption, usage time, and multidimensional AI dependency are related to two-wave changes in subjective well-being (self-esteem and life satisfaction) and ill-being (loneliness, anxiety, and depression). A two-wave longitudinal panel survey of 1,022 South Korean adults was conducted, with data collected in October 2022 (the pre-generative AI era) and March 2026 (the post-generative AI era), providing a prediffusion baseline against which change can be indexed. A multilevel modeling approach was used to examine within-subject and between-subject differences simultaneously. The results revealed that simple AI adoption and daily usage time were largely unrelated to changes in users’ subjective well-being or ill-being. However, a problematic form of AI use—specifically, withdrawal-type dependency characterized by psychological distress or frustration when unable to use AI—was associated with less decline in loneliness, with a suggestive but less robust pattern for depression, over time. These findings indicate that the use of generative AI is neither inherently beneficial nor intrinsically harmful. Instead of focusing merely on adoption or usage time, future research and practice should further examine maladaptive withdrawal-type AI dependency as a potential marker of less favorable mental-health change.

title: Knowing You Seeing Me: The Role of Visual Contact During Video-Conferencing for Emotion Recognition and Mimicry
authors: Michal Olszanowski, Aleksandra Fortuńska, Natalia Frankowska
abstract: This study investigated how asymmetrical visual access in video-conferencing—specifically sender and receiver camera status—affects emotion recognition and facial mimicry. Ninety-one participants viewed bimodal (facial-vocal) or vocal-only displays of four emotions (anger, disgust, sadness, and happiness) while their own camera was either on or off. Recognition accuracy, intensity ratings, and facial muscle activity electromyography (EMG) were recorded. Results revealed that bimodal displays significantly enhanced recognition accuracy and perceived intensity compared with vocal-only signals, except for sadness. Emotional mimicry was most pronounced for affiliative displays (happiness and sadness) and was significantly stronger in the bimodal condition. Exploratory analyses suggested that the awareness of being observed (self-camera on) intensified smile-like reactions and improved the recognition of sadness. These findings suggest that mutual visibility facilitates emotion recognition and affiliative mimicry. The self-camera may function as a cue for public self-awareness, possibly sharpening sensitivity to an interlocutor’s emotional signals. This research highlights the importance of multimodal communication in sustaining interpersonal synchronization during remote interactions.

title: Does Fear of Missing Out Precede Problematic Internet Use, or the Reverse? A Two-Wave Cross-Lagged Study of Taiwanese Adolescents
authors: Chi-Jung Sui, Mingchuan Hsieh, Ming-Hsueh Tsai
abstract: Fear of missing out (FOMO), online social comparison, and problematic Internet use (PIU) are consistently correlated in adolescents, and influential models treat FOMO as a motivational antecedent of problematic use. This temporal ordering, however, has rarely been tested against its reverse. We analyzed the first two annual waves of the Taiwan i-Generation Panel Study ( N = 8,311; Grade 7 to Grade 8; 49 percent girls) and estimated a latent cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) of PIU symptoms, FOMO, and online social comparison, using the survey weights and jackknife replicate standard errors. PIU symptoms predicted later FOMO (standardized β = 0.12, p < 0.001), and FOMO predicted later PIU ( β = 0.06, p = 0.017). The difference between the two directions was not statistically significant (Δ β = 0.06, 95 percent confidence interval [−0.01, 0.12], p = 0.093), and this remained so across eight analytic specifications, in which the estimates varied depending on the measurement model. FOMO and social comparison also predicted each other in the primary model but not in the ordinal sensitivity analyses, whereas social comparison did not predict later PIU, and all cross-lagged associations were small. These prospective associations do not support treating FOMO only as an antecedent of problematic use, because problematic use also preceded FOMO. A two-wave design cannot separate within-person change from stable differences between adolescents, so the findings describe prospective associations and await replication across three or more waves.

title: When Messages About Science Get Old, Does Humor Make Them New?
authors: Scarlett Sijia Liu, Nathan Walter
abstract: In high-choice media environments, repeated persuasive messages often produce message fatigue, marked by disengagement and resistance. This research examines whether humor can mitigate fatigue. Across two studies spanning distinct domains and cultures, findings reveal a conditional role for humor. Study 1 ( N = 268) shows that humor reduces fatigue only among low-trust individuals. Study 2 ( N = 406) demonstrates that effectiveness depends on message design: incongruity humor reduces fatigue more than aggressive humor, particularly when paired with suggestive (vs. imperative) language. Collectively, humor is not a universal remedy but a strategic tool whose impact depends on audience characteristics and message features.

title: A Meaning-Oriented Pathway From Science Fiction to Science Interest: The Role of Entertainment Motivations and Experiences
authors: Yao Yao, Fangzhou Zhou, Jian Raymond Rui
abstract: Characterized by imaginative and futuristic themes of science and technology, science fiction (sci-fi) may foster science interest, yet theory-based empirical evidence remains scant. Drawing on entertainment theories, we conducted a cross-sectional survey (Study 1, N = 517) and a retrospective survey (Study 2, N = 300). Results showed sci-fi engagement bridged both hedonic and eudaimonic motivations to science interest, while only eudaimonic motivation was directly linked to it. Recalling sci-fi (vs. comedy) films elicited stronger eudaimonic appreciation, which predicted heightened intentions to seek science information. Findings suggest that sci-fi can facilitate interest development mainly through a meaning-oriented pathway.

title: Prevalence or Threat? How Misinformation Interventions Shape Veracity Discernment and Trust in Scientists
authors: Myojung Chung, S. Mo Jones-Jang, Betty S. Lai
abstract: Science misinformation poses two distinct problems: promoting inaccurate scientific beliefs and undermining trust in scientists. Yet little research has examined the psychological mechanisms through which interventions may address both problems. An experiment ( N = 832) compared accuracy prompts and threat-focused and efficacy-focused forewarning, examining perceived misinformation prevalence and threat as mediators. Both forewarning messages increased perceived prevalence and threat, but only threat was associated with better veracity discernment and greater trust in scientists. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing how widespread misinformation seems from how harmful it feels when examining how interventions shape veracity discernment and trust in scientists.

title: The Hype Versus the Reality of Generative AI in Elections: The Case of the 2024 Indian Elections
authors: Simon Chauchard, Kiran Garimella
abstract: The 2024 Indian General Election was defined by pervasive warnings that generative AI would unleash a tsunami of deepfakes and fundamentally destabilize democratic processes. To empirically test these predictions, we analyzed over 5.5 million messages from more than 6,000 WhatsApp groups, obtained through a large-scale data donation project in India. Our findings reveal a profound disconnect between pre-election hype and ground truth: generative AI constituted only about 1.1 percent of the image dataset once corrected for the measured recall of our detection pipeline, a figure we treat as a lower bound, with no evidence of a viral “deepfake” epidemic. Furthermore, a qualitative taxonomy of this content reveals that the technology was rarely deployed for deception. Instead, it was primarily utilized for “phatic” labor—automating the production of hyper-stylized “Good Morning” greetings, religious iconography, and patriotic art. We argue that AI adoption was constrained by technological friction and by economic incentives, as traditional “cheapfakes” remained comparatively more cost-effective alternatives for political actors. These results challenge the prevailing focus on the threat of AI-driven messaging, suggesting that the technology may not always lead to epistemic disruption, but rather to the efficient reproduction of existing social rituals.

title: When Elections End, Does Incivility? Examining Online Incivility Perceptions Across Four National Elections
authors: Eliza Mitova, Laia Castro, Pamina Syed Ali, Michael Amsler, Yuan Zhang, Frank Esser
abstract: Political incivility violates democratic, deliberative, and politeness norms, with repercussions for societal health. These repercussions are amplified in today’s digital environment, where social media platforms facilitate the expression and spread of incivility at an unprecedented global scale. Because incivility is subjective and context-dependent, its perception can only be fully understood through a joint consideration of individual factors and contextual conditions. To this end, we advance a three-level framework for examining incivility perceptions which conceptually maps the interdependence between micro-level individual factors and macro-national and meso-electoral specifics. We examine how well this framework plays out for perceptions of political incivility on social media across four nations with different media and political systems (Brazil, Spain, Switzerland, and the United States), drawing on a two-wave panel survey in the weeks leading up to and following their national elections (2022–2024). Contrary to our expectations, perceptions were highest in Brazil and the United States, the latter being the context whose permissive opportunity structures we expected to be most desensitizing. Change over the electoral period followed three distinct pathways: perceptions increased in Brazil, remained stable in Spain, and decreased in the United States and Switzerland, a pattern consistent with how decisively each electoral contest was resolved. Individual dispositions showed no uniform effects. Instead, their influence varied with national contexts. The findings suggest that online incivility perceptions may be primarily shaped by macro- and meso-level conditions, specifically the national political context and its electoral landscape. We conclude by discussing what the results imply for democratic resilience in increasingly uncivil information environments.

title: Ideological (a‐)symmetries in moral judgments of online hate
authors: Vladimir Bojarskich, Meltem Yucel, Lindsay Hahn, Tobias Rothmund
abstract: Political ideology is key in how we react to social and political events, but how does it predict moral judgments of online hate? The contextual symmetry hypothesis suggests that conservatives and liberals condemn online hate similarly when it targets ideologically favored groups. The generalizable asymmetry hypothesis proposes that conservatives, compared to liberals, are less condemning of hate comments regardless of the target. Across experiments in Germany ( N = 903) and the United States ( N = 490), we found consistent evidence for the contextual symmetry account: Conservatives and liberals differ in their sensitivity toward online hate depending on the target and ground their moral judgments on perceptions of the aggressor's responsibility and the victim's vulnerability and suffering. These findings suggest that public divisions over hate speech regulation may reflect ideological differences in perceptions of victim vulnerability, suffering, and perpetrator responsibility, rather than a general conservative tendency to condone online hate.

title: A sentiment-based approach to measuring multidimensional party positions using transformer
authors: Hung H. V. Nguyen
abstract: Existing automated position scaling models from texts rely on the conflict-driven assumption, forcing models to search the linguistic space for differentiating features between political subjects. This leads models to conflate rhetorical styles with political sentiments when subjects are not inherently conflictual. This article introduces ContextScale, a sentiment-based position scaling framework leveraging pre-trained Transformer models to predict policy topics and political sentiments and measure topic-specific position scores across multiple policy dimensions at the sequence level. ContextScale offers an alternative way to gauge party positions, focusing on how political texts express attitudes toward policy issues rather than on contrast between actors. Validity tests demonstrate its ability to capture nuances in party positioning and its adaptability across languages, text domains, and theoretical models.

title: Quality Controls Can Improve the Replicability of Survey Experiments Using Online Nonprobability Panels
authors: Edgar Cook, James Martherus, Alexander Podkul, Anja Kilibarda
abstract: Scholars across multiple disciplines have documented challenges related to replicability, often referred to as a “replication crisis.” While a range of explanations exist, some have argued that the growing reliance on online nonprobability samples contributes to replication failures. At the same time, concerns have mounted regarding the quality of these samples, as inattentive, duplicate, or fraudulent respondents can bias estimates and diminish effect sizes. In this research note, we replicate three well-known survey experiments, using data collected from three separate online nonprobability panels (N = 6,000). We compare the “off-the-shelf” samples with subsets that pass a series of attention and fraud checks and that remove duplicate respondents. We find that all three experiments replicate in terms of direction and significance across the full samples, but in two out of three cases, effect magnitudes are replicated only once low-quality responses are removed.

title: The sound of persuasion: Using generative AI to identify gender gaps in political influence
authors: Ethan C. Busby, Lisa P. Argyle, Parker Davis, Joshua R. Gubler, Bryce Hepner, Christopher F. Karpowitz, Alex Lyman, Justin Olcott, Jessica R. Preece, David Wingate
journal_full: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Women often experience a deficit in persuasive influence, particularly in contexts like politics, where expectations about women’s behavior may conflict with gendered expectations about the domain and role. In spite of this widespread pattern, the mechanisms behind the gender gap in persuasion are difficult to isolate and test in dynamic political conversations. Women may be less persuasive simply because role-based expectations prompt others to afford women less authority when speaking about politics generally or about some political topics. Alternatively, women may be less persuasive because they tend to use linguistic patterns or rhetorical strategies that are less effective. Using an original AI-based approach, we put 4,300 human subjects into realistic, real-time phone conversations with an AI agent. These agents were randomly assigned either a masculine or feminine gendered conversation topic and a male- or female-sounding voice, allowing us to manipulate topic and perceptions of speakers’ gender while holding constant other elements of rhetorical content and strategy. After validating the experimental treatments, we find no direct effects of perceived gender of the AI agent, as cued by voice. However, gender affects other important aspects of the persuasive interaction. Research subjects were more likely to be persuaded about the masculine topic (defense spending) than the feminine topic (aid to the poor). Additionally, women research subjects were, on average, more persuaded than men. To the extent that men and women emphasize different topics in political conversations and have different discussion partners, these dynamics are likely to shape women’s political persuasive influence.
